lessons.title: Idioms you can't translate
lessons.goal: Understand and use five everyday idioms to tell a story colourfully.

tip.title: Meter la pata, tomar el pelo…
tip.body: Idioms are fixed chunks: change one word and they sound odd, so learn them whole and conjugate only the verb. These are understood almost everywhere Spanish is spoken: tomar el pelo (to pull someone's leg, literally to take their hair), estar en las nubes (to have your head in the clouds), meter la pata (to put your foot in it, literally to put in your paw), no tener pelos en la lengua (to speak your mind, literally to have no hairs on your tongue) and costar un ojo de la cara (to cost an arm and a leg, literally an eye from your face). Note the possessive: in Spanish it's el pelo and la cara, not mi pelo: ¿Me estás tomando el pelo?

lines.name: Lucía
lines.t: ¿Qué te pasa? Llevas toda la mañana en las nubes.
lines.n: What's up with you? You've had your head in the clouds all morning.

lines.t: Es que anoche metí la pata en la cena con los padres de mi pareja.
lines.n: It's just that last night I put my foot in it at dinner with my partner's parents.

lines.name: Lucía
lines.t: ¿En serio? Cuéntamelo todo. ¿Qué dijiste?

lines.t: Pregunté si el cuadro del salón lo habían comprado en un mercadillo… y resulta que les costó un ojo de la cara.
lines.n: I asked if they'd bought the painting in the living room at a flea market… and it turns out it cost them an arm and a leg.

lines.name: Lucía
lines.t: ¡Me estás tomando el pelo! ¿Y qué te dijeron?
lines.n: You're pulling my leg! And what did they say?

lines.t: Su madre, que no tiene pelos en la lengua, me dijo que tenía un gusto pésimo. Bueno, no hay mal que por bien no venga: ahora ya sé lo que piensa.
lines.n: Their mother, who speaks her mind, told me I had terrible taste. Well, every cloud has a silver lining: now I know what she thinks.

lessons.title: How cool! Slang around the world
lessons.goal: Recognise and use the regional words for 'cool' and react like a local.

tip.title: Guay, chido, chévere, copado
tip.body: Every country has its own word for cool. Spain: guay. Mexico: chido and padre (¡Qué padre!, nothing to do with fathers here). Colombia: chévere and bacano (bacán is the usual form in Chile and Peru); chévere is also typical of Venezuela and much of the Caribbean. Argentina: copado and bárbaro. They're informal: great with friends, odd in a job interview. Genial and increíble work everywhere and in any register, so they're a safe bet. Mexicans also say ¿Neta? (Really?) and ¿Te late? (Do you fancy it?).

phrases.note: Colombia, Venezuela and much of the Caribbean.
Colombia. Bacán is the usual form in Chile and Peru.

phrases.n: Great! I think it's a brilliant idea.

lines.name: Diego
lines.t: ¿Ya viste? Conseguí boletos para el concierto del sábado. ¿Te late venir?
lines.n: Did you see? I got tickets for Saturday's concert. Do you fancy coming?

lines.t: ¡Qué padre! Claro que sí. ¿Quién toca?
lines.n: How great! Of course. Who's playing?

lines.name: Diego
lines.t: Una banda de aquí de Monterrey que está buenísima. Te va a encantar, neta.
lines.n: A band from here in Monterrey that's really good. You're going to love it, honestly.

lines.t: ¿Neta? Mi amigo Andrés, que es de Bogotá, dice que son muy chéveres.
lines.n: Really? My friend Andrés, who's from Bogotá, says they're really cool.

lines.name: Diego
lines.t: Jaja, ¿chéveres? Así dicen en Colombia. Aquí decimos que están bien chidos.
lines.n: Haha, chéveres? That's what they say in Colombia. Here we say they're really chidos.

lines.t: Pues en Madrid dirían que son muy guais. Lo importante es que vamos juntos.
lines.n: Well, in Madrid they'd say they're really guais. The important thing is we're going together.

lessons.title: Getting to the point
lessons.goal: Speak frankly in colloquial Spanish: cut to the chase, agree and push for action.

tip.title: Al grano, en el clavo, las pilas
tip.body: To cut to the chase, say Vamos al grano (let's get to the grain); to tell someone to stop beating about the bush, No te andes por las ramas (don't wander through the branches). Dar en el clavo is to hit the nail on the head, and ponerse las pilas (to put your batteries in) means to get your act together. No tiene ni pies ni cabeza: it makes no sense at all. Argentines use che to get attention, dale for OK and sin vueltas for straight out; remember the voseo imperatives with the stress at the end: mirá, decime, pensalo.

phrases.t: No te andes por las ramas.

phrases.n: You hit the nail on the head.
phrases.note: Spain often: Has dado en el clavo.

phrases.t: Me tengo que poner las pilas.
phrases.n: I need to get my act together.
I didn't sleep a wink last night.

phrases.t: Este plan no tiene ni pies ni cabeza.

dialogue.title: A frank word in Buenos Aires

lines.name: Valeria
lines.t: Che, ¿tenés cinco minutos? Quiero hablarte del proyecto.
lines.n: Hey, have you got five minutes? I want to talk to you about the project.

lines.t: Sí, claro. Vamos al grano: ¿qué pasa?
lines.n: Yes, of course. Let's get to the point: what's up?

lines.name: Valeria
lines.t: Mirá, te lo digo sin vueltas: el plan del jefe no tiene ni pies ni cabeza.
lines.n: Look, I'll tell you straight out: the boss's plan makes no sense at all.

lines.t: Diste en el clavo. Yo tampoco entiendo cómo vamos a terminar todo en dos semanas.
lines.n: You hit the nail on the head. I don't understand how we're going to finish everything in two weeks either.

lines.name: Valeria
lines.t: Exacto. Hay que ponerse las pilas y proponerle otra cosa. ¿Me ayudás a armar una propuesta?
lines.n: Exactly. We need to get our act together and suggest something else. Will you help me put a proposal together?

lines.t: Dale. Anoche no pegué ojo pensando en esto, así que mejor resolverlo cuanto antes.
lines.n: OK. I didn't sleep a wink last night thinking about this, so we'd better sort it out as soon as possible.

lessons.title: Ser or estar? It changes the meaning
lessons.goal: Use adjectives whose meaning changes with ser and estar.

tip.title: Ser listo, estar listo
tip.body: With some adjectives, ser and estar give completely different meanings. Ser listo is to be clever; estar listo is to be ready. Ser aburrido is to be boring; estar aburrido is to be bored. Ser rico is to be rich; estar rico is to taste delicious (Esta sopa está riquísima). Ser malo is to be bad (a bad person or poor quality); estar malo is to be ill, mainly in Spain, or to have gone off (El pescado está malo). Similarly, el vino es bueno means it's good-quality wine, while el vino está bueno means it tastes good. Careful: about a person, está bueno / buena means he or she is attractive, so use with care! The adjectives agree: a woman says Estoy lista, Estoy aburrida.

phrases.t: La película es aburrida, por eso estoy aburrido.
phrases.n: The film is boring, that's why I'm bored.

phrases.t: El abuelo está malo y no puede venir.
phrases.n: Grandad is ill and can't come.

lessons.goal: Follow travellers from four countries comparing their slang in a Colombian hostel.

story.title: Noche de salsa en Cartagena
story.intro: Camila, who runs a hostel in Cartagena, invites three guests from Spain, Mexico and Argentina to a salsa night.

lines.name: Camila
lines.t: ¡Bienvenidos al hostal! Esta noche hay salsa en la terraza. ¿Se animan?
lines.n: Welcome to the hostel! There's salsa on the roof terrace tonight. Are you up for it?

lines.name: Javi
lines.t: ¡Qué guay! Yo me apunto, aunque bailo fatal.
lines.n: How cool! Count me in, although I'm a terrible dancer.

lines.name: Rodrigo
lines.t: ¿Guay? Ah, como decimos en México: ¡qué padre! Yo también voy.
lines.n: Guay? Oh, like we say in Mexico: how great! I'm going too.

lines.name: Valentina
lines.t: ¿Padre? ¡Qué gracioso! En Argentina diríamos que es un plan bárbaro. Dale, voy.
lines.n: Padre? How funny! In Argentina we'd say it's a brilliant plan. OK, I'm in.

lines.name: Camila
lines.t: Y aquí en Colombia decimos que es un plan muy chévere. Pero ojo, que esta salsa no se come: ¡se baila!
lines.n: And here in Colombia we say it's a really cool plan. But careful, this salsa isn't for eating: it's for dancing!

lines.name: Javi
lines.t: ¿Me estás tomando el pelo? Yo pensaba que íbamos a cenar.
lines.n: Are you pulling my leg? I thought we were going to have dinner.

lines.name: Rodrigo
lines.t: Ay, Javi, siempre estás en las nubes. Hay cena antes, ¿verdad, Camila?
lines.n: Oh, Javi, you've always got your head in the clouds. There's dinner first, right, Camila?

lines.name: Camila
lines.t: Claro, a las ocho. Y después, todos a bailar, que con este calor la noche va a estar bacana.
lines.n: Of course, at eight. And afterwards, everyone dancing, because in this heat the night's going to be great.

lessons.title: I put my foot in it
lessons.goal: Own up to a mistake, apologise convincingly and propose a fix.

phrases.n: Sorry, I put my foot in it.

phrases.t: Me pongo las pilas ahora mismo.
phrases.n: I'll get my act together right now.

branch.title: The missed meeting
branch.scene: You work in an office in Bogotá. Yesterday you forgot an important meeting with a client. This morning your colleague Gonzalo, who had to handle it alone, comes over to your desk.
branch.name: Gonzalo

start.t: ¡Hola! ¿Qué pasó ayer? Te estuvimos esperando toda la mañana en la reunión con el cliente.
start.n: Hi! What happened yesterday? We were waiting for you all morning in the meeting with the client.

choices.t: Ay, perdona, metí la pata: se me pasó por completo.
choices.n: Oh, sorry, I put my foot in it: it completely slipped my mind.
What meeting? Nobody told me anything.

denial.t: ¿Cómo que nadie? Te mandé el correo y te lo recordé el lunes.
denial.n: What do you mean, nobody? I sent you the email and reminded you on Monday.

choices.t: Tienes razón, estaba en las nubes. Lo siento mucho.
choices.n: You're right, I had my head in the clouds. I'm really sorry.

choices.t: Pues yo no lo vi. No es mi culpa.
choices.n: Well, I didn't see it. It's not my fault.

apology.t: Bueno, son cosas que pasan… aunque el cliente se fue bastante molesto. Me tocó explicarle todo a mí.
apology.n: Well, these things happen… although the client left pretty annoyed. I had to explain everything to him myself.

choices.t: Te propongo una cosa: hoy mismo lo llamo y le pido disculpas.
choices.n: Here's what I suggest: I'll call him today and apologise.

choices.t: Bah, ese cliente se queja por todo. Tampoco es para tanto.
choices.n: Bah, that client complains about everything. It's not that big a deal.

careless.t: Mira, te lo digo sin pelos en la lengua: ese cliente es el que nos paga el sueldo.
careless.n: Look, I'll tell you straight: that client is the one who pays our salaries.

choices.t: Diste en el clavo. Me pongo las pilas y lo llamo hoy mismo.
choices.n: You're absolutely right. I'll get my act together and call him today.

choices.t: ¿Me estás tomando el pelo? Es un pesado.
choices.n: Are you kidding me? He's a pain.

fix.t: Me parece muy bien. Pero ojo, quiere el informe para el viernes. ¿Alcanzas a terminarlo?
fix.n: Sounds good. But watch out, he wants the report by Friday. Can you finish it in time?

choices.t: Sí, para mí es pan comido. Esta tarde me pongo con ello.
choices.n: Yes, it's a piece of cake for me. I'll get on with it this afternoon.

push.t: Con un 'ya veremos' no le puedo decir nada al cliente. Necesito una fecha.
push.n: I can't tell the client anything with a 'we'll see'. I need a date.

choices.t: Tienes razón. El jueves por la tarde lo tienes, te lo prometo.
choices.n: You're right. You'll have it on Thursday afternoon, I promise.
Then tell him whatever you like.

good.t: ¡Listo! Así sí. No hay mal que por bien no venga: si le entregamos el informe antes, el cliente va a quedar feliz.
good.n: Great! That's more like it. Every cloud has a silver lining: if we hand him the report early, the client will be happy.
good.outcome: You owned up, apologised and committed to a clear fix, and your colleague is back on your side.

bad.t: Bueno, pues el jefe se va a enterar de todo esto. Yo no pienso cubrirte otra vez.
bad.n: Well, the boss is going to hear about all this. I'm not covering for you again.
bad.outcome: Denying it or brushing it off made things worse. Admitting the mistake (metí la pata) and proposing a concrete fix wins people back.

lessons.title: Tell it with idioms
lessons.goal: Tell a lively story about a blunder in about 90 seconds, using idioms and slang.

culture.title: A slang map of the Spanish-speaking world
culture.body: Spanish is an official language in around twenty countries, and everyday slang changes as you cross borders. To say something is cool, Spaniards say guay, Mexicans chido or padre, Colombians chévere or bacano, and Argentines copado or bárbaro; chévere is also typical of Venezuela and much of the Caribbean. Argentines and Uruguayans use vos instead of tú and sprinkle their speech with che. Classic idioms such as meter la pata or tomar el pelo, on the other hand, are understood almost everywhere, so they're a safe bet wherever you are.

phrases.t: Metí la pata hasta el fondo.
phrases.n: I really put my foot in it.

phrases.t: Total, que al final todo salió bien.
phrases.n: Anyway, in the end it all turned out fine.

free.n: Tell a friend about a time you (or someone you know) put your foot in it: where you were, what happened step by step, how people reacted and how it ended. Use at least two idioms and one slang word for 'cool' or 'great'.
free.hint: Use Primero…, Luego…, De repente…, Al final…; metí la pata (hasta el fondo), estaba en las nubes, me quedé de piedra, no tiene pelos en la lengua, me costó un ojo de la cara, no hay mal que por bien no venga; ¡Qué vergüenza!, guay / chido / chévere / copado.
free.model: El año pasado, en una boda en México, metí la pata hasta el fondo. Primero, estaba en las nubes y no escuché bien el nombre de la novia. Luego, en el brindis, la llamé por el nombre de la ex del novio. ¡Qué vergüenza! Me quedé de piedra. Al final, la abuela, que no tiene pelos en la lengua, se rio y dijo: ¡qué chido, por fin una boda divertida! Total, que no hay mal que por bien no venga.

lessons.goal: Pass to earn your B2 badge and unlock C1.

tip.title: Make your case
tip.body: Sentences come from all eight B2 units, shown in English only: debating and defending your view, meetings, negotiating, the news, technology, health and wellbeing, city versus country life and idioms. Say them in Spanish from memory. Answer in a structured, persuasive way: take a position, back it up (por un lado…, por otro…, además, sin embargo), concede a point (ahí te doy la razón) and round off (en definitiva). Keep idioms word for word, watch ser and estar, and keep going after small slips.
